title: Other crash-retrieval claims, 1947-1965: Aztec, San Agustin, Kingman, Kecksburg
notes: The crash stories other than Roswell, with Stringfield's status reports as the collector. Canon cluster 8 (Newton, GeBauer, Steinman, Good) extends it.

lead.text: Apart from Roswell, the early crash-retrieval stories are allegations: they begin with Frank Scully's account of a disc recovered near Aztec, New Mexico, whose sources were convicted of fraud in 1953, and they were gathered into a literature by Leonard Stringfield's Status Reports from July 1978 to February 1994.

summary.text: Aztec comes first. Scully's Variety columns of 1949 and his 1950 book placed a crash in March 1948 in Hart Canyon, twelve miles northeast of Aztec, with a 99-foot craft and sixteen bodies. His sources were Silas M. Newton, who lectured on it at Denver University in March 1950 as Mr. X, and Leonard GeBauer, the likely Dr. Gee of the book.

The Plains of San Agustin claim rests, by the Air Force's count, on three testimonies: two second-hand, from Vern Maltais and Alice Knight relaying what Grady L. Barnett told them, and one first-hand, from Gerald Anderson, who came forward in 1990.

Kingman, Arizona, 1953 was first investigated and reported by Raymond Fowler from a pseudonymous source and was carried into the retrieval literature by Stringfield; the Del Rio claim of 1948 or 1950 exists only as a one-line entry in Stringfield's chronology.
Kecksburg, Pennsylvania, in December 1965 has a contemporary press report of an official cordon, and it led to federal litigation over the records.

record.text: A one-page FBI memorandum of 22 March 1950 by Guy Hottel, special agent in charge of the Washington Field Office, relays an account of three circular craft about fifty feet across recovered in New Mexico, each with three humanoid bodies three feet tall in metallic cloth, the recovery attributed to high-powered radar interference. It ends: "No further evaluation was attempted."
The FBI describes the memo as a second- or third-hand claim it never investigated, and it became the most-viewed document on the Bureau's Vault reading room after that opened in April 2011.

The Denver Public Library's account of Newton's lecture records his claim that the beings were probably from Venus, between 38 and 42 inches tall, in cloth that could not be torn, and driven by a magnetic propulsion that allowed travel at twice the speed of light.

Newton and GeBauer were charged with swindling Herman A. Flader of $50,000 with a magnetic doodlebug pitched as built on alien technology. The devices were found to be made of surplus military radio parts costing roughly $3.50 each, and the mystery metal Newton supplied to the reporter J. P. Cahn was ordinary aluminium.

Cahn published the exposure in True in September 1952 and August 1956. The pair were convicted of fraud in 1953 and also faced federal charges, and in 1969 Newton pleaded guilty to further fraud over the salting of the Buckhorn Mine in Silver City, New Mexico.

Stringfield delivered the first Status Report at MUFON's ninth annual symposium in Dayton on 29 July 1978, MUFON published the second in January 1980, and the title and copyright pages attest all seven, to February 1994, as his.

Status Report VII of February 1994 acknowledges past funding from the Fund for UFO Research and the cooperation of the J. Allen Hynek Center for UFO Studies, whose scientific director Stringfield consulted on 6 November 1993 about the Roswell body count.

The Greensburg Tribune-Review reported in December 1965 that the Kecksburg landing area was immediately sealed off on the order of US Army and State Police officials and roped off pending Army engineers and possibly civilian scientists; a later edition ran the headline Searchers Fail to Find Object.
NASA stated in December 2005 that experts had examined metallic fragments from the area and found them to be from a Soviet satellite, but that the records of those findings were lost in the 1980s.

Leslie Kean's FOIA request sought records on Kecksburg, Cosmos 96 and Project Moon Dust. Her suit, Kean v. NASA, was filed on 9 December 2003; on 27 March 2007 the court found that NASA had not shown its searches adequate and ordered a joint proposal for search procedures, a partial settlement followed in October 2007, and the case was dismissed on 24 August 2009 on NASA's representation that it had met its obligations.

The Air Force's 1997 report prints Anderson's interview in full at Appendix C, from unedited footage made for the Fund for UFO Research video Recollections of Roswell Part II, and drew the Maltais and Knight statements it analysed from the same footage.

claimed.text: Scully's book alleged a craft 99 feet across with sixteen humanoid bodies, from Venus, working on magnetic principles, with every dimension divisible by nine, which the military had taken for secret research.
In 1974 Robert Spencer Carr claimed that alien bodies recovered near Aztec were stored in Hangar 18 at Wright-Patterson, which drew Air Force denials.

Stringfield revived Aztec in the late 1970s after two decades in which ufologists treated it as dead, arguing that the craft was one of many held by the US military; Status Report V lists it alongside Roswell, Kingman, El Yunque and Brown County. Later defences by Scott and Suzanne Ramsey and Frank Thayer followed, and the town's library ran an Aztec UFO Symposium from 1997 to 2011.

The Kingman account reached print by a documented route: Fowler first investigated and reported it from a source using the pseudonym Fritz Werner, Stringfield cited it in Situation Red in 1977 and in Retrievals of the Third Kind in 1978, and in August 1980 he wrote to Fowler to put questions to Werner, whose written answers of 2 September 1980 are printed in Status Report III.
The Del Rio claim exists as a single index line in Stringfield's chronology: "1948 or 1950: Mexico, near Del Rio, Texas. Air Force officer observed crashed craft and one body."

Barnett never gave an account himself: he died in 1969, and what he saw reaches the record only through Maltais and Knight on camera for the Fund's video, where Knight said "I don't recall the date." Anderson, the one first-hand claimant, described the bodies with the words "I thought they were plastic dolls".

The Kecksburg witness pool was collected by one investigator, Stan Gordon, over four decades. Residents describe an acorn-shaped object about the size of a Volkswagen with hieroglyph-like writing, taken out by a military operation, and John Hays has said since 1990 that as a boy he saw a flatbed truck leave the site carrying it. The same pool supplied the 1990 and 2003 television programmes.
A NASA public liaison officer, Steve McConnell, testified in the Kean litigation that two boxes of papers from the time of the incident were missing.

On the board's reading, Kecksburg is a documented cordon around an undocumented object, and the suit's premise that records should exist rests on Gordon's witnesses, since no document independently establishes a recovery. Both are inferences.

contested.text: The FBI's own position is that the Hottel memo does not prove the existence of UFOs; some believe it repeats a hoax circulating at the time, though the Bureau's files cannot confirm that. The board reads it as a dated marker that the recovery rumour had reached official channels before Scully's book appeared, not as confirmation of Aztec: its three fifty-foot discs are not Scully's one 99-foot disc.

The board treats Aztec as a contamination event rather than a case: a documented fraud supplied specific details, heat-proof material and bodies of 36 to 42 inches at about 40 pounds, that later reappear in supposedly first-hand accounts of other sites, and later Roswell accounts carried the Aztec story. The first part is the board's inference.

Asked in 1980 for facial detail, Kingman's source wrote: "Since it's been 27 years, details like this are pretty foggy and I may even be influenced by other descriptions I've seen or heard in the interim." The board treats the case as a research target rather than evidence for that reason.

Stringfield himself wrote in Status Report IV that public research does not possess proof, and that affidavits, leaked documents and photographs do not constitute it. The board adds that his anonymised case coding, which protected his sources, makes the corpus unauditable, and that indexes built on it, such as the Majic Eyes Only catalogue, inherit the same limits.

The board contrasts the Status Reports with Clear Intent, their contemporary, which sourced every claim to a released government document, and reads Kevin Randle's later case-by-case surveys as an audit that kept named sourcing and rejected the rest. Both are the board's comparisons.

The case against San Agustin came from inside the field: Mark Rodeghier of CUFOS and Fred Whiting of the Fund for UFO Research published The Plains of San Agustin Controversy in 1992, concluding against Anderson. The board's own Tier 3 assessment also asserts, without a cited record, that he submitted a forged document.

The Air Force's 1997 report proposes that Maltais and Knight confused the Plains with San Agustin Pass or Peak, beside White Sands and the Jornada Test Range, where numerous anthropomorphic dummy flights ended, and it read Anderson's account of the recovery as consistent with dummy launch and recovery.
Stringfield's own last report records a source placing the 1947 event just north of Roswell, not on the Plains of San Agustin.

NASA's records disagree with each other on Kecksburg: its 2005 statement attributed the fragments to a Soviet satellite, while its published entry on Cosmos 96 says the fireball's path was probably too steep for an orbital re-entry, that Air Force tracking shows Cosmos 96's orbit decaying earlier than 21:43 UT on 9 December 1965, and that other analyses definitively rule it out.
Del Rio cannot be graded above Tier 3 on the board's own reckoning, since its index entry offers two years and an ambiguous country and no named source has told it consistently.

questions: What sentence was actually imposed on Newton and GeBauer in 1953? The court record has not been found, and the newspaper reports of probation and restitution are unchecked.
What do Scully's 1949 Variety columns say in the original, and did he know his sources were confidence men?
Were any of Stringfield's anonymised informants ever identified by name, and does anyone know who Fritz Werner was?

Does any Pennsylvania State Police or Army Corps of Engineers record of the December 1965 cordon exist, and how does it square with the astronomers who assessed the fireball as a meteor ending over Lake Erie?
What exactly did the Rodeghier and Whiting report find, read in the original rather than as the Air Force cites it?
Does any diary or letter of Barney Barnett's from the time survive?
